scenes.title: Cohort Analysis
scenes.narration: Cohort analysis groups users by when they first joined and then tracks how each group behaves over the following periods, most often to measure retention.

scenes.title: The building blocks
bullets: A cohort is the set of users who first signed up in the same period
We measure behavior by months since signup, not by calendar month
Retention is the share of a cohort still active in a later period
The output is a grid: cohorts down the side, period offsets across
scenes.narration: Cohort analysis rests on a few ideas. A cohort is all the users who first became active in the same period, such as a signup month. We then measure their behavior relative to signup, counting months since they joined rather than the calendar month. Retention is the fraction of a cohort still active in each later period. The classic output is a grid with cohorts down one axis and the number of periods since signup across the other.

scenes.title: Steps to build a retention grid
steps: Find each user's first-activity month to assign their cohort
Join that cohort back to all of the user's activity
Compute the month offset between each activity and the signup month
Count distinct users per cohort per offset, then divide by cohort size
scenes.narration: Building the grid follows four steps. First, determine each user's first-activity month, which fixes the cohort they belong to. Next, join that cohort month back onto every activity record for the user. Then compute the offset, the number of months between each activity and the user's signup month. Finally, count the distinct active users per cohort at each offset and divide by the original cohort size to get a retention rate.

scenes.title: Assigning each user to a cohort
scenes.code:
WITH first_activity AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(activity_date)) AS cohort_month
    FROM events
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
    f.cohort_month,
    COUNT(*) AS cohort_size
FROM first_activity f
GROUP BY f.cohort_month
ORDER BY f.cohort_month;
scenes.narration: First we assign users to cohorts. The CTE finds each user's earliest activity date and truncates it to the month, which becomes their cohort month. The outer query then counts the users per cohort month to give the cohort sizes. These sizes are the denominators we will later divide by to turn raw active counts into retention percentages.

scenes.title: Retention by months since signup
scenes.code:
WITH first_activity AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(activity_date)) AS cohort_month
    FROM events
    GROUP BY user_id
),
activity AS (
    SELECT
        f.cohort_month,
        e.user_id,
        (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM e.activity_date) * 12
         + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e.activity_date))
        - (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM f.cohort_month) * 12
           + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM f.cohort_month)) AS month_offset
    FROM events e
    JOIN first_activity f ON f.user_id = e.user_id
)
SELECT
    cohort_month,
    month_offset,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users
FROM activity
GROUP BY cohort_month, month_offset
ORDER BY cohort_month, month_offset;
scenes.narration: Now we build the retention numbers. The first CTE again tags each user with their cohort month. The second joins every event back to that cohort and computes the month offset by converting both dates to a count of months and subtracting, so an event in the signup month is offset zero and one month later is offset one. The final query counts distinct active users per cohort per offset. Dividing each of these by the cohort size from the previous query yields the retention grid.

scenes.text: Cohort analysis reveals whether newer users stick around better than older ones. It separates genuine retention trends from raw growth that can mask churn.
scenes.narration: Cohort analysis matters because it shows whether newer users retain better than older ones, separating real retention trends from raw growth that can otherwise hide churn.
